name: GFT: November Edition in Mehrauli
description: Grounds for Thought: Mehrauli, November 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought brings researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into rooms full of curious people, where the conversation goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This November in Delhi moves from the hidden mathematics behind everyday intuitions to modern love, from caste and labour to the pleasures of horror cinema, from AI at the margins to the air Delhi breathes.3rd November: Awanish Pandey Is a Second Medical Opinion Always Reliable? The Hidden Maths Behind Every Decision Why does food at an expensive restaurant sometimes taste worse than food at a roadside dhaba? Why are the most attractive celebrities rarely the most talented, and vice versa? Awanish Pandey, Assistant Professor at IIT Delhi's Optics and Photonics Centre and a former researcher at CERN, argues that questions like these are already mathematics in disguise — and that some of our strongest intuitions about the world are built on nothing sturdier than a convincing pattern. No equations, no background required: just curiosity, and a healthy suspicion of things that seem obvious.17th November: Moggallan BhartiHow Does Caste Haunt the Dreams of Modern India and Its Workers? Caste in India doesn't stay confined to its "seemingly societal concerns" — it shapes who gets to labour, how that labour is valued, and what social standing comes attached to it. Moggallan Bharti, Assistant Professor at Ambedkar University's School of Development Studies and a researcher of Dalit politics, argues that the labour theory of value cannot be understood in India apart from the caste structure it's embedded in. This session traces how the unfinished project of Indian modernity has left the country without a sustained, pan-India anti-caste movement — and asks what an inclusive public sphere would actually require.24th November: Keshav Kumar Chaudhary AI for Antyodaya Most conversations about AI centre on innovation, productivity, and economic growth. Keshav Kumar Chaudhary, a youth advocate for digital justice and first-generation learner, asks a different question: what does AI look like from the position of someone still at the margins of India's digital transformation? Drawing on Gandhi's idea of Antyodaya — upliftment of the last person — this session moves from digital access to digital justice, tracing literacy, agency, dignity, and participation as the real tests of whether a technology serves the people furthest from power.

name: GFT: November Edition in Vasant Vihar
description: Grounds for Thought: Vasant Vihar, November 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Thursday evenings. Three very different conversations.12th November: Palak ChananaLove Actually? Attachment Styles, Situationships & the Patterns We Keep Repeating. Why do you keep finding the same kind of person? Why is it so hard to say what you need, or to leave when you meant to, or to stop repeating a pattern you thought you'd already moved past? Palak Chanana, a counselling psychologist and neuro-queer affirmative therapist who founded UnTangle Yourself, draws on anonymised, composite themes from individual and couples counselling to explore how fear, expectation, and past experience quietly shape the way we connect. This isn't a session about finding the right partner or following relationship rules — it's an invitation to get curious about how you love, what you actually need, and what you keep repeating without noticing.19th November: Deborishi GogoiVisceral Pleasures of Viewing Horror Cinema You're gripping your pillow, heart racing, yelling "don't go in there" — and loving every second of it. For decades, film theory explained this through Freud: repression, the unconscious, hidden anxiety. Deborishi Gogoi, a PhD scholar at Shiv Nadar Institution of Eminence working on folk horror and the critique of ideology, argues that account misses the most important part — what watching horror actually feels like, moment by moment, in the body. Through the framing, sound, and editing rhythm of three recent horror films — Suspiria, Midsommar, and The Ugly Stepsister — this session builds the case that horror's pleasure isn't saved for the ending. It's built into the dread itself.26th November: Vasundhara BhojvaidBreathing Delhi: Can a City Hold Air? What does it mean to live in a city where the atmosphere itself feels like confinement? Vasundhara Bhojvaid, Associate Professor of Sociology at Shiv Nadar University, works with a concept she calls "Hawa-laat" — a play on hawalaat, a police lockup, and the physical jolt of Delhi's toxic air. Moving past ecological data into what she calls our "aerial imaginations," this session asks how an invisible hazard like air pollution quietly reconfigures relationships, redraws urban space, and reshapes what survival means in a city that can no longer take its air for granted.

name: Clearing the Smoke and Mirrors
description: In late October, Mumbai's AQI crossed 320 while Delhi sat at 176, its cleanest reading for that date in a decade. So what does it mean when the capital is breathing easier than the coast?Not much, if you ask the people who study this. A single day's AQI is a weather report as much as a pollution report, and one clean week in Delhi is not a solved problem any more than one bad week in Mumbai is a new one. But the comparison is useful, because it puts pressure on the assumption most of us carry around: that this is a Delhi problem, caused by Delhi things, fixable by Delhi alone.We've all done the winter ritual. Complaining about the AQI, feeling what the air does to our lungs, sleep, skin and routines. Every year we're handed the same list of culprits: stubble burning, construction dust, industrial emissions, cars, trucks, garbage fires, landfills, brick kilns, diesel generators and, of course, the wind. The panels shout, the season passes, and by next November we're no clearer on which of these actually matters, or by how much.Atmospheric scientist Dr Mohammad Rafiuddin starts with the hand Delhi has been dealt: a landlocked city on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, hemmed in by the Himalayas, with winter air that sits still. It's a bad hand, but not a unique one, and if cities elsewhere with the same conditions have got their air under control, so can this one. From there we go sector by sector through what is actually in the air we breathe, which sources genuinely move the needle, and why the answer never stops at Delhi's border.The session explores:Why a daily AQI number tells you as much about the weather as about pollutionHow Delhi's geography and winter stillness trap what we put into the air, and why that isn't an excuseWhat's actually in the air, sector by sector: transport, biomass and solid-fuel burning, waste, dust, construction, industry and stubbleWhich sources matter most, by how much, and which solutions would genuinely cut emissions from eachAbout the SpeakerDr Mohammad Rafiuddin is an atmospheric scientist who once built a fog-forecasting system for Bengaluru airport, which means pilots have landed on his maths. He is now Programme Lead – Clean Air at CEEW, where he researches what Delhi's air is made of, how well the city can predict it, and why the answer never stops at Delhi's border. He holds a PhD in atmospheric sciences from the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru, a Post Graduate Diploma in Urban Environmental Management and Law from National Law University, and a BTech in mechanical engineering from Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Hyderabad.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Stories We Carry: Early Christian Practice and Pluralism in India
description: About the LectureLong before the arrivals that dominate the popular account, Christianity had already taken root in the subcontinent and begun to evolve in conversation with everything around it. This lecture introduces that early history through the Southist Syrian Christians — also known as the Knanaya — and the folklore the community still practises and passes on today.Those songs, customs and inherited stories turn out to be a kind of archive. Read closely, they point to the plural worlds in which early Indian Christianity grew: the cultural encounters, the borrowings, the many different ways of belonging that shaped it. Dr Ann Susan Aleyas uses them to move us past the singular narratives that dominate contemporary discourse, towards something considerably more tangled and more interesting.The session explores:The early history of Christianity in the Indian subcontinent, and how much of it predates the familiar accountWho the Southist Syrian (Knanaya) Christians are, and what their folklore preservesHow living traditions carry history that written records often leave outWhat gets lost when a plural history is told as a single storyAbout the SpeakerDr Ann Susan Aleyas is an Assistant Professor in the Department of English at Jesus and Mary College, University of Delhi. She earned her PhD in English from Jamia Millia Islamia, where her research explored the intersections of Christianity in India and print modernity, and her interests also include women's studies and performance studies. With over nine years of teaching experience, she has taught at St. Stephen's College and at Jesus and Mary College, where she now holds a permanent faculty position. She has presented at national and international forums including Soka University in Japan, the Ireland India Institute at Dublin City University, Jamia Millia Islamia and the University of Würzburg, and her publications include contributions to the Encyclopedia of Indian Religions, Studies in Humanities and Social Sciences and The Book Review. An avid reader, she has recently taken to sharing book reviews on Instagram, where she also showcases her love for sarees, and she is a trained Bharatanatyam dancer who hopes to return to her practice soon.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Sacred Streets of Shahjahanabad
description: Beyond the crowded bazaars and familiar landmarks of Old Delhi lies a carefully layered historic city shaped by faith, community, poetry and a distinctive way of urban life. Shahjahanabad was a city of neighbourhoods, markets, sacred spaces and grand residences, each organised according to the social and cultural needs of the people who lived there.This walk journeys through the sacred streets and hidden neighbourhoods of Shahjahanabad to understand how this remarkable Mughal city was planned and experienced. Participants explore the differences between a kucha, katra and gali, discovering how these distinct urban spaces shaped community life and movement through the city. The walk also examines the design of traditional havelis and the architectural principles that created private worlds behind their seemingly modest street-facing entrances.From the remarkable legacy of Digambar Jain Lal Mandir and Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib to the hidden heritage of Naughara and the enduring presence of Fatehpuri Masjid, the walk reveals how different communities shaped the city. A visit to Ghalib ki Haveli adds another layer, connecting Shahjahanabad's streets with the literary and cultural world of nineteenth-century Delhi.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Shahjahanabad as a planned Mughal city and an exploration of how its streets, markets and neighbourhoods developed around communities, occupations, faith and everyday life.Visit Digambar Jain Lal Mandir and explore the remarkable legacy of Delhi's oldest Jain temple while understanding the relationship between sacred spaces and the surrounding urban neighbourhood.Continue to Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib and uncover its powerful story of faith, sacrifice and resilience within the historic landscape of Chandni Chowk.Walk through the historic streets and neighbourhoods of Shahjahanabad while understanding the difference between a kucha, katra and gali, and how these spaces shaped movement, trade, privacy and community life.Explore Naughara and discover its hidden Jain temples and beautifully preserved heritage havelis.Understand how traditional havelis were designed, from their relationship with the street to the organisation of private and shared spaces within, and examine how architecture responded to the social life of the city.Continue through the hidden streets of Chandni Chowk, discovering architectural details and neighbourhood stories that reveal how Shahjahanabad functioned as a living city.Visit Ghalib ki Haveli and step into the literary world of Mirza Ghalib, exploring poetry, culture and everyday life in nineteenth-century Delhi.Visit Fatehpuri Masjid and understand its significance within the urban and commercial landscape of Shahjahanabad.Conclude with a discussion on how faith, communities, neighbourhood planning and architecture came together to create one of India's most remarkable living historic cities.

name: Simple Thinking to Leapfrog in Your Life
description: About the LectureDoes complex thinking actually lead to better outcomes?We live in a world that equates complexity with intelligence. Faced with a difficult problem, our instinct is to add more: more information, more analysis, more process, until we arrive at a sophisticated solution. But more is not always better, and sometimes it gets in the way.Prof. Mukesh Sud explores a different way of approaching the challenges we face in our personal and professional lives. Through stories and real-world examples, he shows how stepping back, asking the right questions and looking at a problem with fresh eyes can reveal surprisingly simple paths forward.Simple thinking isn't about simplistic answers or ignoring complexity. It's about finding clarity amid chaos: identifying what truly matters, questioning assumptions, and focusing your energy on the problem that actually needs solving.The session explores:Why we instinctively reach for complexity, and when it works against usHow stepping back and asking the right questions can reveal simpler paths forwardThe difference between simple thinking and simplistic answersPractical ways to find clarity, question assumptions and focus on the problem that mattersAbout the SpeakerMukesh Sud is a former faculty member at IIM Ahmedabad and was previously an entrepreneur. A visiting fellow at the Judge Business School, Cambridge, he continues to teach at IIM Ahmedabad and Ashoka University. His books, including Leapfrog and Simple Thinking, are national bestsellers and have been translated into many languages.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Be Delusional: Bend Reality To Your Beliefs
description: About the Lecture Join us for a lecture about believing something about yourself long before anyone else does:Kanye West recorded an album with his jaw wired shut. Stallone turned down serious money rather than give up the lead role. What were they running on, years before the proof arrived?The question is whether a certain amount of delusion is rational. Harinder Singh Pelia takes the obvious objection, survivorship bias, we only hear about the ones it worked out for, head-on, and makes the case that belief ahead of evidence is a reasonable bet when your downside is capped and your upside isn't.From there the session moves into what the research actually says: the Pygmalion effect and the Israeli military studies behind it, Bandura on self-efficacy, Vroom's motivation equation. Then into the mechanics, how the confidence-competence loop turns a belief into a skill, and how streaks and the No Zero Days framework keep it running on ordinary days. Expect an interactive turn partway through, built around Maslow's "if not you, then who?", and one concrete assignment to take home.The session explores:Why belief tends to run years ahead of proof, and what that looks like up closeThe survivorship-bias objection, and why capped-downside bets are worth making anywayWhat the research says: the Pygmalion effect, self-efficacy, and Vroom's motivation equationThe confidence-competence loop, and the No Zero Days framework for daily executionBezos's regret-minimisation framework, and the "when-then" trap that keeps people waitingAbout the SpeakerHarinder Singh Pelia is an author and entrepreneur who has led marketing teams at Amazon, Ajio Luxe and Diesel, among others. name: Ghalib Aur Dilli : Poetry ,People & Lost Worlds
description: What happens when a poet's beloved city begins to disappear before his eyes?This is not a conventional Chandni Chowk heritage walk. Instead, we explore Old Delhi through the eyes, words and wonderfully complicated life of Mirza Ghalib—one of the greatest poets of the Urdu language.Ghalib loved Delhi, its culture, its people and its refined social world. But he also witnessed the city undergo extraordinary upheaval, particularly during and after the Revolt of 1857. As Delhi was devastated and its familiar world transformed, the poet found himself grappling with loss, uncertainty and the disappearance of a way of life he had known.Through his letters, poetry and anecdotes, we will explore how Ghalib saw his city, how he responded to its changing fortunes, and what his writings reveal about Delhi during one of the most turbulent periods in its history.As we walk through selected corners of Old Delhi, the city becomes the backdrop to his extraordinary story. The experience concludes at Ghalib ki Haveli in Ballimaran, bringing us closer to the poet, his world and the city that inspired him.Come for Ghalib's poetry, stay for his stories—and discover a very different way of looking at Old Delhi.

name: Straight Lines Are for Rulers: Why It's Okay to Not Have It All Figured Out
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture for anyone whose plan has stopped going to plan:We're told to get the degree, get the job, stay put, marry and have kids, all on schedule. We're also told to live in the moment. Which is it?Nitika Seth has spent twenty years moving between the fashion industry, media and the classroom, from styling and fashion desks at Grazia and Marie Claire to creative direction for brands, and now a deanship. Her argument is that the detours built range, resilience and a kind of wisdom that no textbook hands over. This session is for anyone rethinking a plan that fell apart, weighing a big decision, or working out how to start over, in a career, or in the unglamorous business of making friends at 30 or 40.The session explores:The script: the conflicting messages we're given about planning and living in the momentWhy detours build range, and what moving across fields teaches that no book canStarting over when the plan breaks, including making friends as an adultThe silent archive: the script of keeping the peace, and an optional, anonymous way to contribute to a larger projectAn open conversation with the roomAbout the SpeakerNitika Seth is Dean of the Department of Design at IILM University, with over 20 years of experience across academia, media and the fashion industry. name: Body Language Speaks Louder Than Words@ThePianoMan
description: An OutClass Bar Lecture with Gaurav GillABOUT THE SESSION Every conversation has a second layer. Learn to notice it.Someone says they’re fine, but something feels off. A job candidate sounds confident, but their delivery tells a different story. A first date is going well — or is it? And what can a handshake, a fleeting expression or a change in posture actually tell you?We communicate even when we aren’t speaking. But how much can you really tell from the way someone looks, moves, listens and responds?Join Gaurav Gill, Consultant Psychologist and Body Language Expert, for an eye-opening evening that takes you inside the fascinating world of non-verbal communication. Drawing on real-world investigative experience, forensic psychology and high-stakes interactions, Gaurav will show you how to observe human behaviour with a sharper, more informed eye.What makes this especially interesting? The same principles of behavioural observation used in criminal investigations can also help us better understand everyday interactions — from first dates and friendships to job interviews, negotiations and workplace dynamics.WHO IS THIS FOR?The curious. The observant. The people who love figuring out what makes others tick.Whether you’re navigating dating, building your career, negotiating at work, studying psychology, or simply fascinated by human behaviour, this session will give you a fresh perspective on the conversations happening around you.No prior knowledge of psychology is needed. ABOUT THE SPEAKERFeatured on many podcasts, including Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast, in an episode that has drawn more than 3.2 million views. Gaurav has trained law enforcement personnel and forensic professionals across India, including Delhi Police Crime Branch AHTU, CISF, RPF and GRP, and has delivered expert sessions at institutions including the National Forensic Sciences University and Rashtriya Raksha University. He was also featured on WION analysing world leaders’ non-verbal cues around the 2026 BRICS Summit.Now, he brings these insights out of the classroom and into the bar.WHAT YOU’LL DISCOVER• The face behind the words: Understand facial expressions, gestures, posture and eye movements — and what they may reveal about a person’s emotional state.• Nervousness or something else? Explore the difference between ordinary stress, discomfort and behavioural changes that deserve a closer look.• Can you spot a lie? Challenge popular myths about deception and discover why no single gesture can reliably tell you whether someone is lying.• Read the room: Recognise shifts in engagement, comfort and interaction during conversations, meetings and social situations.• Make a stronger impression: Learn how your own body language can influence how you come across in interviews, presentations, negotiations and everyday encounters.THE OUTCLASS EXPERIENCEWe believe the best conversations don’t always happen in classrooms.The OutClass brings powerful ideas and fascinating people into bars and cafés, creating a space where you can enjoy a drink, discover something unexpected and leave with more to think about — and talk about.Come for the drink. Stay for the thought.One evening. A new lens on human behaviour. And conversations that might never look the same again.

name: K se Karuna: India’s Intellectual Inheritance
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that asks where our political vocabulary, that we use almost every day - actually came from:Liberty, equality, fraternity. Three words that built the modern nation, and all three arrived here from somewhere else. What if the organising idea had come from within South Asia instead?The nation-making of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries settled on that trio, and we have lived inside it ever since: in constitutional safeguards, in the language of rights, in what we understand democratic life to guarantee. Ideas that germinated in the continental world and travelled into the Global South as imports, carrying both a formal-legal meaning and a substantive promise for how people might live together.Pia David turns to a different inheritance. Karuṇā, compassion, is an idea that emerges from within this geography, and it has its own long history of thinking about difference, diversity and ethical living. Not only in the ancient past, but through the reformist and political thought of modern India, where it kept resurfacing in arguments about what a shared life demands.The question the lecture leaves us with is a live one. What would it mean to treat karuṇā not as sentiment but as political method?A way of addressing global conflict, human despair, and the particular poverty that enters political discourse when compassion goes missing from it?The session explores:How liberty, equality and fraternity became the default grammar of modern political lifeKaruṇā as an idea with its own intellectual lineage in South Asia, ancient and modernHow questions of diversity, difference and ethical living were imagined from within this regionWhat compassion offers as a mode of praxis, not just a normative horizon for theory, but something politics could actually doAbout the SpeakerPia David is from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, and is trained as a political scientist. As a Foundation for Universal Responsibility Dalai Lama Studies Fellow in 2023, she worked on Dharma and Dhamma: A Modern Reading of Gandhi and Ambedkar in the Context of Deep Diversity. Her interests span liberal political philosophy and social and political thought from South Asia in the context of the world. She can be found on long walks through forested gardens, tombs and ruins, usually with friends, sometimes in solitude, never without music. Her current favourite is Libertango. She lives in Delhi, wondering about Mir's lament on his exile.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Whose Border Is It Anyway?: Everyday Stories from India's Borders
description: About the LectureWhen we picture India's borders, we picture conflict, army men, terrorists. Where are the people who actually live there?For them, negotiating the border is a Tuesday. It shapes what they eat, who they marry, where they work, which language they slip into, and what they can and cannot carry home.Filmmaker Samarth Mahajan has spent years making films in these places, and this session is a kaleidoscopic journey into India's deepest recesses — through images, video, anecdote and song. We meet people who deal with borders in their own particular ways, and who manage to come out of the darkest possibilities with lightness, humour and hope. Along the way: migration, kinship, environment, and identities that refuse to sit still.The invitation is to look past the media's obsession with "Us vs Them", towards something more complicated and more accurate — a world of "Us and Them".The session explores:What daily life actually looks like when a border runs through itMigration, kinship and fluid identity at India's marginsHow humour and hope survive in places we only hear about during conflictWhy "Us vs Them" is a poor description of the borderlands — and what replaces itAbout the SpeakerSamarth Mahajan is a Mumbai-based filmmaker with a particular interest in narratives from India's border areas. His work includes two national award-winning documentaries: Borderlands (2021), which explores lives defined by India's borders, and The Unreserved (2017), which captures stories from the general compartments of Indian Railways. His films have screened across six continents to favourable reviews and received broadcast and theatrical releases in India. IIT Kharagpur has recognised him as a Young Alumni Achiever. His other passion is organising food walks through the crowded streets of Old Delhi, South Mumbai and Amritsar, and he is currently wrapping his debut fiction short.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Yamuna- A river, A city, A memory
description: The Yamuna has been many things to Delhi — a river, a boundary, a source of life, a sacredpresence, and a witness to the making and remaking of the city.On this walk at the Vasudev Ghat near Kashmere Gate we follow the river through the story of Delhi itself. We look at the floodplains thatonce allowed the Yamuna to breathe, and trace the changing relationship between the river and arapidly expanding city. We explore the many drains that now carry the city’s waste into the river,the challenges of treating that waste, and the difficult question of what happens when a cityslowly turns its back on the river that sustains it.But the Yamuna is more than an environmental story. She is Yamuna Mata — a goddess, a mother, and a deeply loved presence in Hindu mythology. We explore the stories, beliefs and rituals that have shaped the sacred imagination around this river for centuries.And as the evening gathers, we end where the river meets ritual. The walk culminates in the Yamuna Aarti at Vasudev Ghat, held every Sunday evening — an evocative coming together of river, light, music, prayer and memory.As lamps are lit and the aarti unfolds beside the darkening river, the Yamuna becomes, for a brief while, not just the river that flows through Delhi, but the river that lives within its imagination.(Plz note the fee being charged is just for the curated experience & not for entry into Vasudev ghat)

name: Who Does the City Belong To?
description: Who Does the City Belong To?A conversation on public space and the lawYou have probably stood in front of a barricade this year. A road closed with no notice. A park gate locked at night. A station shut, a lane that used to be a shortcut now ending in a guard and a boom. Most of us have learned to route around it without thinking.But there’s a question underneath that almost none of us can answer: what are we actually entitled to in a public space and what happens when that space is closed, fenced or policed?In this edition of The Human City Conversations, we’ll ask what the Constitution actually gives us by way of a right to assemble and to protest. Whether a government can simply take a Jantar Mantar away. Whether there is such a thing as a right to walk in an Indian city, and who in Delhi really has it. And how much of what we call planning is in truth a question of who is expected to justify their presence in public, and who is not.It isn’t a lecture, and it isn’t a complaint session. It’s an hour of conversation, in plain words, followed by your questions put directly to someone who has spent two decades arguing these things in court.About the guestMihira Sood is a lawyer and scholar in the field of women’s rights, and practices at the Supreme Court of India and the Delhi High Court. She has taught at Jindal Global Law School and National Law University Delhi, and holds degrees from NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and Columbia Law School, New York. She was among the youngest members to assist the Justice Verma Committee, whose recommendations reshaped India’s criminal law on sexual violence. She writes and speaks widely on women’s rights, feminist jurisprudence, equality law and civil liberties, and is a regular commentator in the national press. She has recently written a book Courting Equality which focusses on the Landmark Cases in the Battle for Women’s Rights (Juggernaut) traces fifty years of the law’s encounter with women’s lives — from the anti-dowry agitations of the 1970s, through Shah Bano and the Uniform Civil Code debate, to the Nirbhaya movement and its continuing reverberations, and on to the present backlash against the supposed misuse of these very laws.Copies will be on sale at Kunzum on the evening, at 20% off.About the seriesThe Human City Conversations is the live edition of The Human City Podcast, hosted by Ruchita Bansal, which for the past year has asked how Indian cities are planned, built and experienced — and who they are built for. The podcast’s questions, taken off the feed and into a room, in public, in Delhi.The detailsSunday 29 November 2026, 5 PM onwardsKunzum Books, GK-2, New DelhiLimited seats · Tickets on Urbanaut
